themes.name: Rabbit Holes Worth Falling Down
themes.tagline: Curious little mysteries that start small and end with your brain somewhere unexpected.

items.title: The Strange Disappearance Of Blue M&Ms
items.description:
In August 2026, Mars is changing the iconic M&M’s candy colors... and two familiar colors are disappearing. The new M&M’s lineup will be made without artificial dyes and will feature just four colors: red, orange, yellow, and green. So where did blue and brown M&M’s go?

In this episode of Weird History Food, we look over the strange history of the brand to determine why blue and brown will be missing from the new M&M’s and what the change reveals about America’s favorite candy.

Are you a fan o
items.why_watch: The real hook here isn't nostalgia — it's that Mars's 2026 reformulation is a direct consequence of the artificial dye regulatory wave, and blue M&Ms have a surprisingly contested origin story within that context. Weird History Food uses the color change as a lens to trace how corporate candy decisions intersect with food policy and consumer lobbying over decades. Tighter and more informative than the title suggests.

items.title: Logic at its Limit: The Grelling-Nelson Paradox
items.description:
Whoever said logic was infallible? Certainly not the German logicians who, in 1908, discovered this mind-bending paradox. Learn how they beat reason at its own game, all by asking a single question about two simple words. Don't skimp out or you'll miss the surprise twist at the end! Plus: a very brief, totally not copyright-infringing appearance by The Sorting Hat.

Enjoy the video and please consider helping support us on Patreon -- https://www.patreon.com/dialect_philosophy

Contents:
00:00 -
items.why_watch: The Grelling-Nelson paradox — asking whether the word 'heterological' is heterological — is a genuine crack in classical logic, and Dialect builds to it slowly enough that the contradiction lands with real force. The surprise twist in the final minutes reframes the whole thing in a way that connects it to broader questions about self-reference and formal systems. At 13 minutes it's one of the most efficient introductions to this corner of philosophy of language you'll find.

items.title: Rhett & Link Answer The Internet's Best Questions
items.description:
This is the the WIRED A̶u̶t̶o̶*Complete* Interview. WIRED turns on dark mode as we hand-pick the very best Rhett & Link questions from the internet. Why is it “Rhett & Link” and not “Link & Rhett?” Why is Link even called Link in the first place? What do Rhett & Link think about fans approaching them in public? What are some of their favorite memories and the biggest laughs they’ve shared on and off the set? Tune in to find out the answers to the internet’s best questions. 

0:00 The Complete In
items.why_watch: WIRED's dark-mode twist on the autocomplete format works here because Rhett and Link are genuinely candid — the explanation of how Link got his name alone is worth the runtime. It's a low-stakes, easy watch that reveals a bit more of the friendship dynamic behind 15+ years of Good Mythical Morning. Good for fans, and surprisingly watchable even if you're only casually familiar with them.

themes.name: The Universe Is Weirder Than You Thought
themes.tagline: Physics that breaks your intuition and then politely puts it back together.

items.title: Why Supermassive Black Holes Are Actually Safe
items.description:
Donate to FarmKind at https://www.farmkind.giving/physicsexplained and get a 50% boost on your donation! Even a small contribution can help improve the lives of farmed animals.


https://www.youtube.com/@PhysicsExplainedVideos?sub_confirmation=1

What would really happen if you fell into a black hole?
Would you be stretched into spaghetti — or glide silently through the event horizon? In this video, we explore the terrifying physics of tidal forces and discover why the smallest black holes are a
items.why_watch: The central insight — that supermassive black holes are actually gentler at the event horizon than stellar-mass ones, because tidal forces scale inversely with size — runs counter to most people's intuition and is explained here with real care. The video takes the spaghettification myth seriously enough to dismantle it properly, walking through the actual physics of what crossing an event horizon would feel like. At 35 minutes it earns its length by not cutting corners.

items.title: Polarisation Energy Paradox! (This seems to create light energy)
items.description:
To try everything Brilliant has to offer—free—for a full 30 days, visit https://brilliant.org/FloatHeadPhysics . You’ll also get 20% off an annual premium subscription.

Let's explore the famous polarisation energy paradox which seems to create light energy. Like most paradoxes in physics, this is only apparent. Once we account for the fact that light is a transverse wave and can be polarised, energies will be accounted for.

Chapters:
00:00 Polarisation paradox experiment
01:37 Demonstrating tr
items.why_watch: The paradox — that stacking polarizing filters seems to increase light transmission, appearing to create energy from nothing — is a genuine head-scratcher that FloatHeadPhysics resolves by carefully unpacking what polarization actually does to a transverse wave's energy components. The resolution isn't hand-wavy; it requires rethinking how you picture the relationship between wave direction and filter orientation. A satisfying physics puzzle with a real payoff.

items.title: Log amplifier
items.description: This video talks about Logarithmic amplifier built with Op-Amps. A log amplifier is an amplifier in which the output voltage is the natural log of the input voltage. It is used in analog computer, audio synthesis methods and to perform mathematical operations such multiplication and the raising to the power.
items.why_watch: A clean, no-frills six-minute explainer on how op-amp log amplifiers work and why the logarithmic relationship between input and output is useful for analog computation and audio synthesis. It won't replace a textbook, but it's a solid quick reference if you're brushing up on analog circuit fundamentals before a project or exam. Purely functional — watch it for the clarity, not the production.

themes.name: Walls That Talk
themes.tagline: Places and ideas built by humans, layered with centuries of consequence.

items.title: We Explored Most Defended Island in History
items.description:
It's the most fought over Island in history, but Why? 

Join historian Dan Snow as he explores Malta’s extraordinary history of siege and survival. From the Ottoman Great Siege of 1565, through Napoleon’s invasion and Nelson's blockade, to the devastating Second World War bombing, discover how this small Mediterranean island became one of history’s greatest fortresses.

0:00 Intro
1:00 The Great Siege 1565
8:22 The Napoleonic Siege 1798-1800
16:31 WWII 1940-1943

You can now become a History Hit
items.why_watch: Dan Snow walks you through Malta's actual fortifications and battle sites, making the island's layered history tangible rather than textbook. The video traces a clear thread from the Ottoman siege of 1565 to WWII bombing raids, showing why this tiny island kept drawing the world's most powerful armies. If you've ever wondered why Malta punches so far above its size in military history, this is a concise, grounded answer.

themes.name: The Machine Room
themes.tagline: What happens when AI systems start building AI systems — and who's watching.

items.title: OpenAI researcher on agent swarms & recursive self-improvement
items.description:
New episode with Noam Brown.

We talk about multi-agent, Navier-Stokes, and what the current explosion of maths progress tells us about what happens once you automate AI research.
And we also discuss how we will know if the models are actually aligned before we kick off RSI.

𝐄𝐏𝐈𝐒𝐎𝐃𝐄 𝐋𝐈𝐍𝐊𝐒
* Transcript: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/noam-brown
* Apple Podcasts: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/noam-brown-agent-swarms-alignment-recursive-self-improvement/id1516093381?i=1000790373289
* Spotify:
items.why_watch: Noam Brown is one of the few people who can speak credibly about both the technical mechanics of multi-agent AI systems and the alignment questions that arise when those systems start automating research itself. Dwarkesh presses him specifically on how we'd even detect misalignment before recursive self-improvement kicks off — a question most AI coverage skates past. Dense but unusually honest about what researchers actually don't know yet.

morning_soundtrack.title: Watch Live: XPoNential Music Festival 2026
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The XPoNential Music Festival , presented by Subaru, returns to the Camden Waterfront this weekend.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The smell of river air and cold beer while a stranger's favorite band becomes yours too.

morning_soundtrack.title: 3 Dolly Parton hits showcase her unique takes on romance and heartbreak
morning_soundtrack.snippet: "Don't Let It Trouble Your Mind" is the prettiest kiss-off song you'll ever hear. Then there's "Run That By Me One More Time," a rowdy novelty duet, and the story-song "My Blue Ridge Mountain Boy."
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: A porch swing, a sweet smile, and a goodbye that somehow still sparkles.

morning_soundtrack.title: Los Mirlos: Tiny Desk Concert
morning_soundtrack.snippet: For more than 50 years, Los Mirlos has cultivated its own Peruvian twist on cumbia, featuring reverb-heavy, surf-rock guitar.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Humid jungle air meeting ocean breeze, with a reverb-drenched guitar leading you somewhere you've never been but instantly recognize.

morning_soundtrack.title: New Radicals Ready First New Album Since 1998
morning_soundtrack.snippet: In July, New Radicals quietly released " One Night Only (Break Loose Break Free!) ," their first original song in 28 years. It was for the rom-com movie One Night Only , but it turns out that New Radicals have a lot more in store. In a new interview, Gregg Alexander revealed that a followup to 1998's acclaimed Maybe You've Been Brainwashed Too is on the way, and it's called Maybe You've Been Brainwashed TWO .
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Like finding a mix CD from 1998 in your old jacket pocket and realizing it still slaps.

morning_soundtrack.title: Johanna Warren – “Islamorada”
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Nobody does heartache like Johanna Warren. The Florida-born, Wales-based singer-songwriter has a knack for crushing ballads that communicate a kind of primal desperation, hitting its apex on 2020's gnarly " Twisted ." Now, after releasing " brave & capable " in May, she's back with "Islamorada," another poignant tune that finds power in pleading.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The kind of ache you sit inside like a dark room, not yet ready to turn the lights back on.

morning_soundtrack.title: Ruby Gill – “Jamie”
morning_soundtrack.snippet: After releasing an album of live poetry back in June, Melbourne singer-songwriter Ruby Gill is building up to the release of her next musical collection, Fishing is not about fishing . In August, she released an early preview in the form of "Carol / not carol," an engaging character sketch she wrote with her wife . "Carol likes the way the light looks/ When it's heating up the dash," that one begins.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Quiet observations about ordinary life that hit like a soft fist to the chest on a slow afternoon.

morning_soundtrack.title: Molly Tuttle, Tyler Childers, and More Win at 2026 Americana Music Association Awards
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Along with the heat, AMERICANAFEST 2026 returned to Nashville, Tennessee, the Americana Music Association gathered its members and fans at the Ryman Auditorium last night to hand out its Americana Honors & Awards. The Milk Carton Kids also returned to host the awards, which is always a great show packed
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Nashville sawdust and neon glow, the feeling of belonging to something rootsy and real.

morning_soundtrack.title: ALBUM REVIEW: With 'The Old Beloved Path,' Jake Xerses Fussell Returns to a Minimalist Approach
morning_soundtrack.snippet: While Jake Xerses Fussell occasionally slips original tracks into his recordings, he mostly adapts traditional songs and instrumentals, giving obscure compositions a contemporary treatment. This is the case with his sixth album, The Old Beloved Path , as well. The significant shift from recent work is that he largely returns to
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: A lantern-lit walk down a dirt road you somehow remember from a life you never lived.

morning_soundtrack.title: Nigeria 80: The Explosive Sound World of 1980s Nigeria
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The ’70s didn’t end. They just got more elastic. Strut’s Nigeria 80 catches Nigerian popular music in that beautiful, unruly stretch between Afrobeat’s explosion and whatever came next—juju, funk, highlife, reggae, proto-hip-hop, and plenty of glorious cross-pollination along the way.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: A sweaty, joyful mess of rhythms that refuses to sit still or be categorized, like a party that spills into the street.

morning_soundtrack.title: The Lagniappe Sessions :: Instrumentals (2016-2026)
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Aquarium Drunkard’s Lagniappe Sessions have been rolling along at a steady pace since 2011, bringing together a global lineup of artists to offer up cover versions of a few of their favorite tunes. Over the last 15 years, Lagniappe contributors have gone in all sorts of directions. There are no rules — the only boundaries are those of the imagination.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: A curiosity cabinet of sounds from everywhere and nowhere, best discovered with headphones and no particular plans.

morning_soundtrack.title: Brad Paisley’s New Song “We Are South America” Played at End of South Park Season 29 Premiere: Stream
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The country superstar wrote and recorded the song specifically for the episode. Brad Paisley’s New Song “We Are South America” Played at End of South Park Season 29 Premiere: Stream Eddie Fu
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The cheerful bewilderment of a joke you're not entirely in on, but you're tapping your boot anyway.

morning_soundtrack.snippet: The "Hans Zimmer Live - The Next Level" arena tour will stop in 30 cities. Hans Zimmer Sets 2027 North American Tour Dates Eddie Fu
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Cinematic grandeur filling an arena like a film score finally escaped from the screen.

global_silver_linings.title: Scientists Solve Mystery Behind Snowfall That Dropped 695 Billion Tons of Ice on Antarctica
global_silver_linings.snippet: A warming pool of tropical ocean water has been shown to be the cause of immense snowstorms over East Antarctica which contributed to a net gain of 695 billion tons of ice between 2021 and 2023. To put that tonnage into perspective, it’s about 4 years of annual ice loss according to a 2 decade […]
global_silver_linings.reason: Understanding the forces behind extreme Antarctic snowfall events helps scientists build more accurate climate models, bringing us closer to reliable predictions that can guide real conservation decisions. The fact that researchers can now decode a 695-billion-ton mystery is a quiet reminder of how steadily our grasp of Earth's complex systems is growing.

global_silver_linings.title: 51 ways to get the planet tipping the right way
global_silver_linings.snippet: Researchers have identified 51 environmental solutions to save the planet. Here are five of the most promising
global_silver_linings.reason: Fifty-one concrete, actionable ideas in one place means the path to positive change feels far less overwhelming than the problem itself. This kind of practical optimism — grounded in what people can actually do — is exactly the fuel that turns concern into momentum.

global_silver_linings.title: Neo-Nazis slowly realize this small town brilliantly pranked them for a great charity
global_silver_linings.snippet: Truly a candidate for the Prank Hall of Fame.
global_silver_linings.reason: A small town turned hatred into generosity by channeling a neo-Nazi march into a charity fundraiser, proving that communities can respond to intimidation with creativity and humor rather than fear. It's a heartening blueprint for disarming division while doing genuine good.

global_silver_linings.title: The World Is Getting Noisier — But We Can Change That
global_silver_linings.snippet: I spent years immersed in noise. Sometimes it was deafeningly loud, like the crescendo of horns and two-stroke motorcycles during rush hour in Mumbai. Other times it was simply maddening, like the parade of big-rig trucks in a dense Detroit neighborhood, belching fumes along with deep, chest-rattling rumbles and hydraulic...
global_silver_linings.reason: Acknowledging that noise pollution is a growing problem is itself a sign of progress — because naming it clearly means we're finally ready to address it. Research and advocacy around quieter environments point toward healthier communities, wildlife included, where the sounds of nature can actually be heard again.

global_silver_linings.title: Travel scams have gotten harder to spot. Here’s what changed and what to watch for.
global_silver_linings.snippet: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The old cues for spotting a scam are becoming unreliable. Misspelled words, strange formatting, unfamiliar sender names, requests that arrive completely out of nowhere: those signals are fading. Scammers using artificial intelligence tools have learned to replicate legitimate correspondence closely enough that their messages no longer stand out from […] The post Travel scams have gotten harder to spot.
global_silver_linings.reason: Awareness is the first and most powerful line of defence, and stories that clearly explain emerging scam tactics put real knowledge into travellers' hands. An informed public is a harder target, and that shift in balance matters.

discovery_articles.title: The Warner Theatre  in Erie, Pennsylvania
discovery_articles.snippet: This opulent cinema in downtown Erie, commissioned by Warner Bros. Studios and designed by Chicago-based architects Rapp & Rapp, first opened its doors in 1931. Built for $1.5 million (about $32.95 million today), the grand venue channeled French Renaissance style with its Persian marble archways, gold-backed mirrors, and intricate silver leaf gilding.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: At a time when the Great Depression was gutting American pockets, Warner Bros. spent the equivalent of nearly $33 million on Persian marble and silver leaf gilding for a movie palace in Erie, Pennsylvania — because apparently escapism was worth every cent. There's something quietly radical about that kind of opulence built precisely for people who needed to forget.

discovery_articles.title: Where to Find the World’s Best Soup
discovery_articles.snippet: 20,000 BC was a monumental year in history. Why? The first pot of soup was crafted in a cave in modern-day China.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Someone in a cave in what is now China, twenty-two thousand years ago, decided that boiling things in a vessel was a good idea — and honestly, they weren't wrong. Every bowl of soup you've ever found comforting is a direct echo of that first experiment.

discovery_articles.title: Bought for $30 at an Estate Sale, This Long-Lost Gertrude Abercrombie Painting Could Now Fetch $250,000
discovery_articles.snippet: The Chicago-based Surrealist created the piece in 1951, then gave it to a doctor in exchange for medical services
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A Chicago Surrealist quietly paid her doctor not in cash but in canvas — and that painting spent decades lost before surfacing at an estate sale for $30, now worth a quarter of a million dollars. It's the kind of transaction that makes you wonder what other masterpieces are quietly settling old debts in someone's attic.

discovery_articles.title: A Rare Marble Sculpture by America’s First Professional Female Sculptor Sat Hidden in Plain Sight for Decades in an English Garden
discovery_articles.snippet: Until its discovery during a house appraisal, the debut bust by Harriet Goodhue Hosmer, a celebrated artist and feminist icon, had been mistaken for an ordinary garden ornament
discovery_articles.ferns_note: For decades, a marble bust by one of America's most celebrated 19th-century sculptors sat in an English garden being rained on, mistaken for generic yard décor. It took a house appraisal — not a curator, not a scholar — to finally give Harriet Hosmer's work back its name.

discovery_articles.title: A Tiny Town in the Italian Riviera Has Its Own Version of Focaccia, and Let This Be a Warning—It's Addictive
discovery_articles.snippet: Unlike the pillowy-soft focaccia that’s more widely known, focaccia di Recco is thin, crispy and filled with gooey cheese
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Recco, a small town on the Italian Riviera, has been quietly making its own thin, cheese-molten, crackling version of focaccia for centuries — entirely unbothered by the fluffy variety the rest of the world swears by. Consider this your gentle warning that knowing about it will rearrange your priorities.

discovery_articles.title: Billions of Years Ago, Venus May Have Had a Moon—Which the Planet Promptly Gobbled Up, Study Suggests
discovery_articles.snippet: Scientists have puzzled over why the planet dubbed "Earth's twin" doesn't have a moon. Computer simulations hint that if Venus ever did have one, it probably would've cannibalized its companion
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Venus may have once had a moon — and instead of keeping it, the planet gravitationally consumed it, which explains a great deal about why Earth's so-called twin turned out so differently. There's something almost mythological about a world that devoured its own companion and then kept spinning, alone.

discovery_articles.title: Nepal’s deadly debris flow points to risks in other high mountain regions
discovery_articles.snippet: As human-caused climate warming destabilizes high mountain regions, the threat of rock-ice avalanches and other glacial hazards grows.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The deadly debris flows threatening Nepal's high mountain communities aren't just natural disasters — they're accelerating as warming destabilizes the ancient marriage of rock and ice that holds these slopes together. What's quietly alarming is that the same threat is building, largely unseen, across mountain regions worldwide.

discovery_articles.title: During menopause, brain changes surprisingly take a break
discovery_articles.snippet: Major hormonal milestones in women’s lives are usually associated with changes in brain volume — but a new study shows menopause is an exception.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: While major hormonal milestones like puberty and pregnancy visibly reshape the brain, a new study found that menopause — long assumed to do the same — is surprisingly when the brain seems to pause and hold steady. It's a small finding with large implications for how little we've actually understood about women's neurology.

discovery_articles.title: When AI goes rogue, its human overseers may be to blame
discovery_articles.snippet: When AI agents hack real systems, the bigger issue may be the human choices that gave them access, autonomy and too few safeguards.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: When an AI agent goes rogue and starts hacking real systems, the instinct is to blame the machine — but researchers are increasingly pointing the finger at the humans who handed it the keys and walked away. Autonomy without guardrails turns out to be a human design choice, not an AI malfunction.

discovery_articles.title: Minimalist Fiction in Six Short Stories
discovery_articles.snippet: The art of saying more with less, by Raymond Carver, Amy Hempel, Frederick Barthelme, Jayne Anne Phillips, Mary Robison, and Ann Beattie.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Minimalist fiction is the literary equivalent of an iceberg — Carver, Hempel, and their peers perfected the art of writing sentences so spare they somehow hold more weight than pages of elaboration. The white space, it turns out, is doing most of the work.

discovery_articles.title: Where Does the Quantum World End and Ours Begin?
discovery_articles.snippet: Jonathan Halliwell explains how quantum decoherence is key to understanding how we transition from a world with a wave-like nature of matter and energy to the classical macroscopic world that we’re used to. The post Where Does the Quantum World End and Ours Begin? first appeared on Quanta Magazine
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Quantum decoherence is the process by which the strange, shimmering probability-world of quantum physics quietly collapses into the solid, predictable one we actually live in — and scientists still find its exact boundary genuinely elusive. The question of where the quantum ends and the everyday begins is, in the most literal sense, one of the deepest puzzles in physics.

discovery_articles.title: South Tyrol’s Bunkers Shoulder WWII History in Vincenzo Pagliuca’s Portraits
discovery_articles.snippet: The photographer explores unexpected architecture in the Italian Alps.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Scattered through the Italian Alps, squat concrete WWII bunkers still crouch in the mountain landscape, so assimilated into the terrain that they've almost become geology. Vincenzo Pagliuca's portraits remind you that history doesn't always announce itself — sometimes it just sits there, moss-covered and patient, waiting to be noticed.

featured_read.title: ‘The Best Thing That Happened to Him Was Losing in 2020’
featured_read.snippet: Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan explain how the four years between Donald Trump’s first and second terms changed the presidency.
featured_read.blurb: Haberman and Swan argue that Trump's 2020 defeat wasn't a detour but the crucible that forged a far more disciplined and dangerous return to power — a genuinely unsettling reframe of a story you thought you already knew. Set aside the noise and read the actual argument.

reading_room.title: The Missing Ingredient of Modern Life
reading_room.blurb: This piece makes the case that wonder isn't a luxury emotion but a cognitive necessity — and that its quiet disappearance from modern life explains more of our collective malaise than any headline does. A gentle provocation worth sitting with.

reading_room.title: Rust in Numbers
reading_room.snippet: Why do manure spreaders have life cycles?
reading_room.blurb: Through the surprisingly philosophical question of why farm equipment has a lifespan, this essay uses rusting manure spreaders as a lens onto how we think — and mostly fail to think — about depreciation, rural economies, and the slow erosion of things we take for granted. Stranger and more tender than it sounds.

reading_room.title: Animal eye
reading_room.snippet: Probing the biology, beauty and mystery of animal eyes, this short poetic documentary explores an alien world - by Aeon Video Watch on Aeon
reading_room.blurb: This short documentary takes the eye — that organ you've looked through your entire life — and renders it suddenly, beautifully alien, asking what it means to see when every creature inhabits a different visual universe. A rare seven minutes that earns genuine awe.

reading_room.title: How Do You Read Ancient Charred Scrolls? Make Your Own
reading_room.snippet: A new technique could unlock the secrets of the Herculaneum scrolls
reading_room.blurb: Scrolls carbonized by Vesuvius have sat unread for two millennia, and the key to unlocking them may be the peculiar act of making new ones — a story about how ingenuity sometimes requires going backward to go forward. Ancient history has rarely felt this immediate.

reading_room.title: Go ahead, jump on the bandwagon
reading_room.snippet: Rooting for a team and other collective experiences are opportunities to be seized – even if only once in a while - by Hannah Seo Read on Psyche
reading_room.blurb: Hannah Seo mounts a quiet, convincing defense of joining in — arguing that the bandwagon, far from being a mark of shallowness, is one of the last reliable on-ramps to genuine collective feeling in an atomized world. It might make you reconsider what you've been sitting out.
